e: Borrowed from obsolete Dutch rijcksdaler (modern rijksdaalder), after early modern German Reichsthaler.
q: At all other times they would receive the regular salary of thirty rix-dollars monthly.
1803, [Author Unknown], Medical Journal — Volume IX, page 539:

Such had the business become before Lord Somerset left, that in 1821 no less than 196 horses were shipped mostly to India, for military remounts by cavalry officers. The declared value was 56,980 rix dollars, which the then currency represented, an average of about £20 per head, or a total of £4,273.
1902 February 28, “The Horse in South Africa”, in The Agricultural Journal and Mining Record, volume 4, number 26, page 828:
The Dutch monetary system of a rix-dollar or rijksdaalder of 48 stuiver was continued [in Cape Province] by the British in the early nineteenth century.
1962, Robert Andrew Glendinning Carson, Coins: ancient, mediaeval & modern, page 533:

e: From obsolete forms of Dutch rijksdaalder.
